newsitem.title: USA: Gore pressed to bar drilling in Utah monument.
newsitem.headline: Gore pressed to bar drilling in Utah monument.

text.p: Wilderness groups have urged the White House to stop the Interior Department from allowing an oil company to drill in the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in Utah, a green group official said Wednesday.
The department's Bureau of Land Management (BLM) was set to clear the way this month for DuPont Co subsidiary Conoco to explore for oil in the monument.
"Based on the information we have to date, it looks like it will be approved," said Robert Hendrix, chief of the bureau's fluid minerals branch.

The Grand Staircase-Escalante land was set aside last year by President Clinton to protect the scenic redrock canyon area from a proposed coal mine. When he named the site, Clinton said the government would honor valid existing leases.
Conoco believes the land could hold more than a hundred million barrels of oil.

Environmental groups have tried to block Conoco's plans, but failed to stop the state of Utah from granting permits for the company to drill on state leases in the monument area. They now want Vice President Al Gore to step into the fray.

"We're trying to get the public to contact Vice President Gore ... because BLM lacks the backbone to protect the monument," said Scott Groene, issues director for the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance.
"BLM has turned into an advocate for this drilling project at this point," he said. "They've really glossed over the environmental impacts."
The agency had planned to approve or deny the drilling permit by July 1, but because it was flooded with comments on its environmental review, the decision was postponed.

Groene said if BLM approved the permit, the environmental groups would appeal, but he added that stopping Conoco would be difficult through the appeal process. "Our ace in the hole is not the legal remedy, it's the political," he said.

Gore has yet to respond to a June 5 letter by the Utah alliance and four major environmental groups urging him to "act to ensure that the Bureau of Land Management heed the president's call to protect the monument by denying Conoco's application to drill this well."
White House officials were not immediately available to comment on the controversy.

Conoco's 10-year leases were set to expire this year. In a bid to hold on to the property for a possible land swap, the company asked the Interior Department to stop the clock on its leases. When the department refused, the company applied for a permit to drill, in the hopes that the government would then suspend the leases.
But Conoco has no specific plans to drill on the federal land. "We can't make any firm plans until we know what the decision is," Conoco's Denver spokesman John Bennitt said.
